seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: Thanks for your card just received. I am afraid this affair bores you. I intend to pursue the matter, so that I shall be obliged if you will send the documents to the persons I mentioned. I sent a set also to Mr Devlin MP c/o House of Commons. If I knew the name and address of my parliamentary representative (my father is domiciled in College Green division) or even the number of his cell I would send them to him. If you have doubles of some of the documents and enough to make up an understandable collection might I ask you to send them to my father: John Joyce c/o George Lidwell, solicitor, Upper Ormond Quay, Dublin. These people are not so irremovable as you think. Mr Bennett (if the rumours afloat here be correct) has just been summarily removed by the Foreign Office to a post in Panama (where the hats come from) in consequence of the protests of the Swiss legation in London against his behaviour here. Gone he is and Mr Carr too. I saw them off the field. But I have by no means done yet. If I can find it I shall enclose a song which is very popular in Zurich drawingrooms. Against de Gourmont’s remark may I quote the homely proverb concerning dogs and fleas? And, in excuse, may I explain the matter to you from another standpoint?

When that grant was made to me (I may say that it did not deserve all the talk made about it nor did it compensate me at all for the ten years of worry I had been put to) I understood from Mr Gosse’s suggestion that I should write newspaper articles and from its non-renewal (a gift of £100 once in his life to a writer may perhaps be useful, at present prices, for a few months but no more) that it had been made to me with another intention. I am now satisfied that I have done much more than I was paid for and in a manner consonant to my own dignity. In no other country would a writer who can point to such a press be, as I am, a beggar living on charity. The shame is not mine, however. And the friendly interest and encouragement of a score of men of letters (for which I am most grateful) does not counterbalance the hostile opposition of the most ignorant and cowardly rabble in the world. I have beaten them to their knees twice before and will do so again.

Please thank Mr Rodker and his friends for their interesting articles, and send me the February number if you have it. With this I send you a review of the Neue Zürcher Zeitung. The translation of Exiles (Verbannte) was published this morning. Mr Linati wants to translate it into Italian.
We are kneedeep in snow here. Will you please let me know how the affair gets on?

note.p: JJ had been embroiled in legal proceedings after a British consular official in Zurich, Henry Wilfred Carr (1894-1962) – who had performed in an Oscar Wilde play put on by the Zurich acting troupe, the English Players, of which JJ was co-founder and business manager – loudly insulted and threatened JJ in the British Consulate in May 1918 over a minor dispute about money owed for tickets to a performance. JJ sued Carr in the cantonal court for money owed, and Carr counterclaimed for salary and expenses. JJ initially won a judgment (LII 421-23), but then unsuccessfully pursued Carr for additional damages for slander, and was ordered to pay court costs, which he refused to do. JJ sought help from British Acting Consul-General, Andrew Percy Bennett (1866-1943), and from Sir Horace Rumbold (1869-1941), the British Minister in Berne, but without success. He came to believe that Rumbold and Bennett were instigating boycotts of the English Players’ performances, and he wrote a statement, dated 28 April 1919, setting forth the history of perceived outrages (LII 438-40).

JJ asked Pound and others, including his London literary agent J.B. Pinker, to circulate the statement and other documents to influential persons (LII 440-41), but Pinker cautioned that the statement might trigger libel proceedings. JJ could not see why he should not make known “such gross and dense abuse of public trust” (LII 442). He had more success with his New York publisher B.W. Huebsch, who showed the statement to several persons in the United States, and with Padraic Colum (1881-1972), who was now in America. Informed by Colum of JJ’s predicament, Scofield Thayer (1889-1982) – a wealthy financer of the New York magazine The Dial – contributed $700 to JJ’s cause, and Thayer’s friend, James Sibley Watson, Jr. (1894-1982), gave another $300 (LI 124-25; Ellmann, JJ 457-58). For an excellent account of the litigation, which finds that JJ’s legal position was stronger than had previously been thought, see Judge Conrad L. Rushing, “The English Players Incident: What Really Happened?” James Joyce Quarterly, vol. 37, no. 3/4 (Spring-Summer 2000): 371-88. For a discussion of the activities of the English Players, based on previously unexamined archival sources, see William Brockman and Sabrina Alonso, “Exit Carr,” James Joyce Online Notes no. 15 (December 2019) (http://www.jjon.org/joyce-s-environs/players).

div.note: On JJ’s behalf, Pound contacted H.G. Wells (1866-1946) and Augustine Birrell (1850-1933), author, barrister, and former Chief Secretary for Ireland (Pound/Joyce 153-55). He also wrote Rumbold on 11 April 1919 to caution that “you can find no surer means of making a few converts to Bolshevism or to the more violent revolutionary factions than by continuing or permitting to continue the persecution of James Joyce by the Zurich officials within the sphere of your influence” (LII 437). If the fear of revolution was not enough, Pound added that he might have to launch a “publicity campaign” on behalf of JJ, who “is doing in [Ulysses] what Flaubert attempted but did not quite bring off in ‘Bouvard and Pecuchet’” (LII 438). These dire prospects did not stir Rumbold. Pound continued to try to assist JJ, but he felt hobbled by the lack of “a clear statement of MAIN facts,” as he wrote JJ circa 1 May 1919. “FER Chrrisst’s sake realize that you have given me no ‘case’ to present” (Pound/Joyce 153).
Joseph Devlin (1871–1934) was an influential member of the Irish Parliamentary Party in the British House of Commons, and later a Nationalist Party MP in the Parliament of Northern Ireland.

The Member of Parliament for College Green Division, Dublin, in 1919 was Seán Thomas O’Kelly. He had been returned in the 1918 United Kingdom general election that saw the Irish Parliamentary Party routed and a landslide victory for Sinn Féin. O’Kelly served as Ceann Comhairle of the First Dáil.

John Stanislaus Joyce (1849-1931) was the father of JJ and nine other surviving children with his wife, Mary Jane Murray. He grew up in Cork and later moved to Dublin, where he held a number of jobs and was awarded the post of Collector of Rates for his political work on behalf of candidates in the general election of 1880. An ardent supporter of Charles Stewart Parnell, his personality, humor, and persiflage strongly influenced JJ, who employed him as a model for Stephen Dedalus’s father, Simon, in A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man and Ulysses.

Bennett had been transferred to a post in Panama, at a higher rank, and not because of the JJ affair. Carr had left Switzerland. The official whom JJ called “Sir Whorearse Rumphole” soon became ambassador to Poland (Ellmann, JJ 458). JJ administered literary punishments by making Carr one of the two English soldiers who menace and assault Stephen Dedalus in the brothel district in the “Circe” episode of Ulysses, and Bennett their sergeant-major. Rumbold he cast as a “Master Barber” whose semi-literate letter offering his services as a hangman to the sheriff of Dublin is read out, to the contempt and ridicule of the pub drinkers, in the “Cyclops” episode (U 12.412-42).

It is uncertain what remark Pound quoted from Remy de Gourmont (1858-1915), French Symbolist poet, novelist, and critic. The “card” JJ had “just received” from Pound has not come to light. Pound had recently published a “Remy de Gourmont Number” of The Little Review, vol. 5, nos. 10-11 (February-March 1919), with essays by himself, Frederic Manning, John Rodker, Richard Aldington, and others. The issue also contained the concluding portion of the “Lestrygonians” episode of JJ’s Ulysses (58-62).
“He that lieth down with dogs, shall rise up with fleas” (Benjamin Franklin, Poor Richard’s Almanack [Mount Vernon, VA: Peter Pauper Press, 1936], 11).

Authors W.B. Yeats (1869-1939) and Edmund Gosse (1849-1928) had been instrumental in 1915 in obtaining for JJ a subsistence grant of £75 from the Royal Literary Fund (see JJ to Pound, 14 July 1915, notes). In August 1916, with help from Pound, Yeats, and others, JJ also obtained a grant of £100 from the British Civil List (see JJ to Pound, 14 September 1916, notes; Ellmann, JJ 390-93, 405-06). At the time of the subsistence grant, Gosse was displeased that JJ had given no statement of loyalty to the Allies in the war. Gosse apparently hinted later that the grant from the Civil List implied some obligation, perhaps to be available for military service. One of JJ’s reasons for founding the English Players was to demonstrate patriotism in a bloodless fashion (Ellmann, JJ 423).

JJ’s novel A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man – published as a book in the United States in December 1916 and in England in February 1917 – received favorable reviews from a number of noted writers and critics (see JJ to Pound, 30 March 1917, notes).

The Little Review, vol. 5, no. 9 (January 1919) contained a symposium called “‘Exiles’: A Discussion,” with contributions by John Rodker, Israel Solon, Samuel A. Tannenbaum, M.D., and “jh” (Jane Heap, co-editor of The Little Review) (20-27). Rodker (1894-1955), an English writer, poet, and publisher of modernist authors, observed of Exiles: “The play is very romantic, poetical in a manner rare among plays…. It was no small achievement of Mr. Joyce to have made dramatic such very pure cerebration, and that with a touch so delicate that no most intricate part of the mechanism has suffered by the inquisition” (21). The issue also contained the opening portion of the “Lestrygonians” episode of Ulysses (27-50). Rodker, who succeeded Pound as London editor of The Little Review, later assisted Harriet Shaw Weaver with her Egoist Press edition of Ulysses (1922) by renting a room in Paris from which he distributed copies to purchasers (Ellmann, JJ 505-06 n.).
For the February-March 1919 number of The Little Review, see note 7 above.

The clipping JJ included with this letter was probably “Ein englisches Drama,” a review of Verbannte in the Neue Zürcher Zeitung for 31 March 1919. Several years before it was performed in English, Exiles was premiered in German on 7 August 1919 in Munich.

JJ’s Exiles was published in English by Grant Richards in London and by B.W. Huebsch in New York in May 1918. The play was translated into German by Hannah von Mettal as Verbannte: Schauspiel in drei Akten (Zurich: Rascher & Cie, 1919). Slocum and Cahoon state that Verbannte was “[p]ublished in March 1919 in an edition of 600 copies, at the expense of the author” (John J. Slocum and Herbert Cahoon, A Bibliography of James Joyce [New Haven: Yale University Press, 1953], 115). JJ says here, however, that it was published on 1 April 1919.

Carlo Linati (1878–1949), Italian writer and translator of English fiction, translated Exiles into Italian as Esuli and published it in Il Convegno, vol. 1, nos. 3-5 (April, May, June 1920): 27-52, 27-46, 22–37.
